title: 3-Read Friday #4: Lesson Efficiency, Observation Thinking, and AI-Proof Assessment
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Issue four opens with Barton's candid admission that Jo Castelino's post on lesson "Rush" describes his own first twelve years of teaching — trying to tick every box of a good lesson while quality suffered from ropey routines. He then covers Tom Sherrington's breakdown of his own thought process during lesson observations, which Barton says he'll build directly into his coaching practice, particularly Sherrington's habit of sitting with a student rather than circulating and his three-way split of curriculum, individual, and collective issues. He closes with Daisy Christodoulou's argument against the popular claim that if ChatGPT can complete an assessment, the assessment itself must be flawed. Two of the three items concern the practice of teaching and coaching itself — efficient routines and observation technique — making this issue lean toward Practice & Culture even though the Christodoulou piece is a substantive curriculum-assessment argument.
points: Barton admits Castelino's description of a rushed, box-ticking lesson structure matches his own practice for over a decade, crediting her with practical fixes.
He singles out Sherrington's habit of sitting next to a student during observations, rather than circulating, as an idea he plans to adopt.
He frames Christodoulou's piece as "dismantling" the popular claim that AI capability alone proves an assessment needs to change, treating it as a much-needed corrective.
quotes: The opening section of this post perfectly describes what my lessons used to look like for the first 12 years of my career (and probably beyond, if I am honest).

Jo goes on to make some super practical suggestions about how we can become more efficient in our lessons, saving precious minutes that allow us to spend time on things that will make a difference to our students.
I particularly like the idea of sitting down next to a student (instead of the busy, and no-doubt distracting, circulating I currently do).

This post from February is brilliant for confronting (and dismantling!) the claim that if tools like ChatGPT can write quality essays and solve complex maths problems at the click of a button, then we need to radically change the type of assessments we give our students.
I really enjoy Daisy and Chris’ No More Marking newsletter, and in particular their reflections on the implications of AI on the way we assess students.
